In the accompanying GitHub repository, detailed vignettes with R code and result output can be found for the https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/tutorial_rmu_sum_score_reliability.html and https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/tutorial_calculating_rmu_bandit.html examples, as well as an additional https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/tutorial_calculating_rmu_gonogo.html not presented here. Here, we focus on how to apply and interpret RMU and refer readers to the linked vignettes for more detailed code and results.

Example 1: Measuring mouse lengths & mean scores

Imagine we measure the length of 5000 mice five times each. Every time we measure a mouse, we will get a slightly different measurement (have you tried holding a mouse with one hand and holding a ruler in the other?). To improve the accuracy of our measurements, for each mouse we will take the mean length across the five measurements. This is exactly what the arithmetic mean was initially used for: 16 th and 17 th century astronomers took the mean of multiple measurements to reduce measurement error (Plackett, 1958).

To simulate this mouse measurement dataset, we generated true lengths for each mouse using a normal distribution random number generator with a mean of 10cm and variance of 3cm (i.e., true score variance; 𝜎 2 𝜃 = 3). Next, for each mouse, we simulate 5 measurements from a normal distribution. The mean of the random number generator is set to each mouse's true score and the variance set to 2cm (i.e., measurement error variance; 𝜎 2 𝜀 = 2), generating five "measurements" for each mouse.

We also simulated 5 additional "retest" measurements for each mouse to evaluate test-retest reliability. Because we know the true score and measurement error variances, we can analytically compute the reliability of the resulting mean scores using the following formula: 𝜎 2 𝜀5 = 3 (3+2/5) = .88 (Lord & Novick, 1968, p. 86).

We can confirm numerically that the squared correlation between simulated mean and true scores is .89 -it is not exactly .88 due to sampling error. If we format the simulated data so each mouse has their own row and we have five columns for each measurement, we can compute coefficient alpha as .88 using the covariances between measurements.

To estimate RMU, we first fit a Bayesian measurement model. We fitted a multilevel model with a fixed intercept (the average length across all mice), a random intercept for each mouse (that mouse's deviation from the average) and a residual error term (the measurement error variance). We used the brms R package to fit the model using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling (Bürkner, 2017). We ran four chains (independent runs of the sampler) of 1,000 posterior draws each, so after pooling chains the posterior for the random intercepts is a matrix with 5,000 mouse rows and 4,000 posterior draw columns. RMU is then computed by correlating random pairs of these columns, yielding 2,000 posterior draw correlations.

Code Snippet 1 shows the code needed to fit the brms model and pass the fitted object to the rmu() function, which extracts the random intercept posterior draws and computes RMU. We use the random intercepts because reliability concerns how mice differ from one another; adding the fixed intercept (a constant shared by all mice) would give each mouse's absolute length but would not change the correlations between draws because we add the same constant to all values. We used brms's default weakly informative priors, which have negligible influence on the subject-level posteriors with 5,000 mice. Our dataset (df) is in a long format: each row is a single measurement, with a measurement variable (the value) and a mouse variable (subject ID), and thus the same mouse ID appears on five rows.

Code Snippet 1. R code for brms multilevel model and RMU estimation brms_model = brm( measurement ~ 1 + (1 | mouse), data = df, chains = 4 ) library(gbtoolbox) rmu(brms_model)

The posterior mean of RMU (the average of the 2,000 posterior draw correlations) is .89, with a 95% highest density continuous interval (HDCI; the narrowest interval containing 95% of the draws) of .88-.89. In this example, each mouse's estimated length derived from the multilevel model random intercepts was almost perfectly correlated with its mean score (r = 1.00), and thus should have the same reliability as mean scores described above. Alternatively, reliability can be estimated directly from the model's variance parameters: substituting posterior means of the random intercept variance (3.12) and residual error variance (2.01) into the equation above gives 3.12 (3.12+2.01/5) = .89. The previous formula can also be applied to each posterior draw of the random intercept and error variances to construct a posterior for reliability, which may yield a slightly different point estimate.

In this example, coefficient alpha and RMU both give us accurate estimates of classical test theory reliability for mean scores. The primary benefit of RMU, however, is that it can be applied more broadly and we can flexibly adjust our model to handle a wider range of modelling scenarios. This can be illustrated by making a few minor changes to the simulation in the next section.

Fussy mice and short rulers

Suppose we now turn to a second breed of mouse: longer (13 cm on average), with the same true score variance (𝜎 2 𝜃 = 3) and measurement error variance (𝜎 2 𝜀 = 2). However, these mice are considerably less patient. Each mouse tolerates somewhere between two and five measurements before wriggling free, so the number of measurements per mouse now varies. To make matters worse, the lab's ruler is only 15 cm long. Lengths beyond 15 cm are recorded as ">15 cm", meaning they are right-censored. We repeated the simulation with all other parameters unchanged; 19% of measurements were right-censored.

This scenario illustrates the benefit of a flexible approach to modelling and estimating reliability. One could compute alpha from pairwise-complete covariances between the five measurement occasions, but the result would describe the reliability of a five-measurement mean, overstating reliability for mice measured fewer times, and it would treat '>15 cm' as if it were exactly 15 cm, ignoring censoring. RMU, by contrast, requires no workarounds: the multilevel model naturally accommodates varying numbers of measurements per mouse, and can be adapted to account for censoring.

The censored multilevel model is shown in Code Snippet 2. We first created a variable flagging which measurements are right-censored and then passed it to brms via the cens() term. The model then treats each flagged measurement as "at least 15 cm" rather than exactly 15 cm when estimating that mouse's length.

Code Snippet 2. R code for brms censored multilevel model and RMU estimation df$censored = ifelse(df$measurement == max_ruler_length, "right", "none") brms_model_censored = brm( measurement | cens(censored) ~ 1 + (1 | mouse), data = df, chains = 4 ) rmu(brms_model_censored)

To obtain a benchmark value, we computed the correlation between the posterior means of each mouse's random intercept from the test and retest simulations, which was .83. This is lower than the previous simulation due to the lower number of measurements per subject and censoring. RMU accurately recovered this estimate (RMU = .82, 95% HDCI [.81, .83]).

Example 2: Reinforcement Learning

While there are well-known and straightforward methods for estimating reliability for mean scores, methods for computa-tional model parameters are not well established. In Example 2, we will illustrate how RMU can be applied to a reinforcement learning model fitted to fluctuating bandit data collected by Pike et al. (2026). We will compare reliability estimates from RMU, empirical reliability, split-half and test-retest methods to illustrate similarities and differences between these quantities in practice.

Task, Data, and Model

In the fluctuating bandit task, on each of 200 trials, participants chose one of four images. After each choice, they could receive a reward (green tick), a punishment (red cross), both, or neither. Reward and punishment probabilities fluctuate throughout the task, so participants must continually update their reward expectations. In total, 547 individuals completed the task at time 1, and 115 were retested two weeks later. Participants were recruited and tested online. We fitted a four-parameter hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement learning model using the bandit4arm_4par function from the hBayesDM R package (Ahn et al., 2017; Seymour et al., 2012). Models were fitted using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling via a cmdstanr backend (4 chains, 3,000 warm-up iterations, which are discarded, and 4,000-7,000 sampling iterations per chain; Gabry et al., 2023).

The model assumes that participant's choices are guided by separate reward and punishment expectations for each option, updated after every trial. Each participant has four parameters. Reward sensitivity and punishment sensitivity scale how strongly rewards and punishments are valued (Aylward et al., 2019; Krypotos et al., 2022). Reward learning rate and punishment learning rate govern how quickly expectations are updated after each outcome. Expectations for unchosen options decay toward zero, so older information about options that have not been sampled recently is gradually discounted. The full model specification and Stan code are given in the https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/applied_example_pike/02_02_pike_2026_bandit.html#model-description.

Estimating reliability

To estimate RMU, we fitted the model to the complete time 1 dataset (N = 547). Empirical reliability was computed from the same complete time 1 fit as RMU. To estimate test-retest reliability, we fitted the model separately to the time 1 and time 2 data from the retest subsample (N = 115) and correlated the posterior mean estimates between time points. To estimate split-half reliability, we divided the complete time 1 data into first-and second-half datasets of 100 trials each, fitted the model to each half, and computed the Spearman-Brown corrected correlation between the resulting posterior means.

Fitting the Bayesian reinforcement learning model to the complete time 1 dataset yields posterior distributions for each participant's two learning rate and two sensitivity parameters. These posteriors are illustrated in Figure 1A; each curve represents our uncertainty about a participant's estimate. Figure 1B illustrates the RMU posterior draws: each row shows the correlation between two random sets of posterior draws, which is repeated many times to build up a posterior distribution for RMU.

Comparison of reliability estimates

Reliability estimates from each method are presented in Figure 1C. Empirical reliability estimates are not shown as these were within .005 of RMU, illustrating that these two approaches yield very close point estimates when estimated on the same posterior draws, with small differences expected at finite sample sizes (see Theoretical Properties of RMU). Empirical reliability, however, provides no uncertainty interval.

RMU exceeded test-retest reliability for all four parameters, by between .13 (reward sensitivity) and .40 (punishment sensitivity and reward learning rate). This highlights that these methods answer slightly different questions. RMU (and splithalf) reliability aim to quantify reliability within a single session, whereas test-retest reliability also measures temporal stability over two weeks. Changes in true scores, such as practice effects or strategy alterations on retest, will lower test-retest reliability (Revelle & Condon, 2018). That RMU and split-half estimates were more similar and both higher than test-retest reliability supports this explanation. Differences between testretest and RMU estimates were not driven by selection bias: we found similar effects when estimating RMU and split-half reliability on the smaller retest subsample (see the https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/applied_example_pike/02_02_pike_2026_bandit.html#retest-sample-n-115 in the GitHub repository). In summary, RMU is not equivalent to test-retest reliability: a parameter can be precisely estimated within a session but vary substantially between sessions.

Agreement between RMU and split-half methods was mixed. For punishment learning rate and reward sensitivity, uncertainty intervals overlapped. For punishment sensitivity and reward learning rate, RMU estimates were .19 and .16 higher, respectively, and the intervals did not overlap. Some discrepancy is expected. RMU assumes the computational model is correctly specified, and split-half assumes that the measurements are parallel (i.e., same true score and measurement error variance in each split-half estimate). A limitation of splithalf reliability is that the model for the second-half dataset does not account for learning that occurred during the first half of the task. This is less problematic for bandit tasks with separate blocks with different stimuli (e.g., Yamamori et al., 2023), unlike the task used here. Another limitation of splithalf reliability is that the resulting point estimate depends on how the data are divided -a source of variability that likely contributed to its lower accuracy and precision relative to RMU in Simulation Study 2.

This comparison also highlights a practical disadvantage of test-retest reliability. Retest designs require inviting participants back for a second session, which inevitably leads to attrition. Because test-retest reliability can only be computed for participants with data at both time points, the available sample is often much smaller. Here, only 115 of the 547 participants contributed to the test-retest estimates. RMU and split-half reliability, by contrast, use the complete time 1 sample, so they are more precisely estimated: the 95% uncertainty intervals for test-retest reliability were around two to five times wider than those for RMU. Although this retest sample was relatively large, retest studies of computational tasks often include around 50 participants, such that confidence intervals can span poor to excellent reliability, limiting their usefulness (Karvelis et al., 2023; Mkrtchian et al., 2023). Most importantly, the benefit of RMU and split-half methods is that they do not require retest data at all.

Additional considerations for reporting and applying RMU

RMU estimates can be quite uncertain, particularly in small samples, and this uncertainty should be reported. The simplest approach is an uncertainty (credible) interval: our rmu() function returns a highest density continuous interval (HDCI) at a user-specified level (95% by default). This function also outputs the RMU posterior draws, which allow uncertainty to be communicated in additional ways. One option is to report the posterior probability that reliability falls within conventional, if somewhat arbitrary, thresholds (e.g., Kline, 2000). For example, for punishment learning rate, the posterior probability that reliability was poor (< .60) was 34%, and the probability that it was acceptable (.60-.80) was 66% (i.e., 34% and 66% of the RMU posterior draws fell in these ranges). No RMU posterior draws exceeded .80, so there was effectively no support for good reliability. This information can be presented in a https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/applied_example_pike/02_02_pike_2026_bandit.html#table-posterior-probability-rmu-falls-in-each-band for multiple parameters. Another option is to plot the full posterior density or histogram for each parameter, showing the most plausible values in a continuous manner (an example is provided https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/applied_example_pike/02_02_pike_2026_bandit.html#plot-posterior-density-of-rmu-shaded-by-band).

Because RMU is computed from the posterior draws themselves, it inherits any problems with posterior sampling, and RMU should only be interpreted once standard diagnostics are satisfactory. Before computing RMU, researchers should check that chains have converged (e.g., R-hat < 1.01), that effective sample sizes are adequate, and that there are no warnings about divergent transitions (Gelman et al., 2021). When such problems arise, the usual remedies apply: increasing the number of warm-up iterations or the sampler's target acceptance rate (adapt_delta), reparameterising the model (e.g., using a non-centred parameterisation for subject-level parameters), or specifying more informative priors (Gelman et al., 2026). Persistent problems may indicate that the model is poorly identified for the available data, and we would then discourage reporting of reliability coefficients derived from the model. For additional guidance on Bayesian workflows for model building, fitting and selection, we refer readers to the following resources (Gelman et al., 2026; Hess et al., 2025; McElreath, 2020; Schad et al., 2021).

If model parameters will be transformed for downstream analysis (e.g., log-transforming learning rates), reliability should be estimated for the transformed parameters. For RMU, this means transforming the matrix of posterior draws before computing RMU (see https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/applied_example_pike/02_02_pike_2026_bandit.html#does-rescaling-parameters-change-reliability-estimates for an example). RMU does not require normally distributed posteriors, but transformations may be justified on other grounds. In some cases, researchers may fit multiple models and select the "best" based on some criterion (e.g., PSIS-LOO, BIC, WAIC). Where this is done, one can report RMU for multiple models as a sensitivity analysis.

Simulation Studies

Study Aims

We conducted three simulation studies to investigate the performance of RMU across different generative models commonly used in behavioural science: the linear factor model (Study 1), the signal detection theory model (Study 2) and the reinforcement learning model (Study 3). We characterize the performance of RMU on several metrics, including bias, coverage and overall accuracy. In studies 1 & 2, we additionally compare the performance of RMU to alternative reliability estimation approaches. We evaluate all methods across different simulation sample sizes, different numbers of items or trials, and different reliability levels (including zero reliability).

Our primary objective is to provide initial evidence of RMU's performance under ideal situations, where the generative models are correctly specified and assumptions met by the generated data. This initial study is not designed to comprehensively test the robustness of RMU to unmodelled data features, such as non-normality, censoring or outliers, which could be investigated in future work (Heinze et al., 2024).

In the first simulation study, we examined the linear factor model because there is a vast literature on reliability estimation for these models. This allows us to compare the performance of RMU to existing methods for these models, including alpha and H. We then evaluated RMU's performance for two alternative generative models without established model-based methods for estimating reliability, as this is where RMU has the potential to make the greatest contribution.

General Methods

All analyses in this section are fully reproducible via the accompanying GitHub repository (https://github.com/giac01/8_bayes_reliability), which includes Docker and Singularity containers for running the scripts in a consistent computational environment.

Estimand

The estimand is the target reliability value for a given simulation condition (Morris et al., 2019; Siepe et al., 2024). To our knowledge, true classical test theory reliability cannot be calculated analytically from the simulation parameters for studies 1-3. We therefore estimated it by simulation. For each simulation iteration, we generated two datasets from the same set of simulated subjects, fitted the Bayesian model to each dataset independently, and computed the correlation between the resulting posterior mean estimates. Because each subject's true parameter values are identical across the two datasets, the datasets constitute parallel measurements, and this correlation corresponds to the second definition of reliability given in the Reliability Primer (the correlation between two sets of observed scores). The estimand for each condition was then the mean of these test-retest correlations across all iterations in that condition. Study 1 employs an additional estimand for comparing different reliability estimators, explained in that section.

In the conditions where population reliability is zero (all item loadings equal to zero in Study 1; sensitivity SD = 0 in Study 2), the simulated estimand fell within ±.006 of zero. Because confidence intervals for coefficient alpha and coefficient H are bounded below at zero, an estimand of exactly zero could never be covered, making coverage uninformative for these estimators. We therefore set the estimand to .001 in these conditions, and applied the same adjustment to the maximal reliability estimand used in Study 1.

Performance Measures

Performance of the point estimates was summarised using root mean squared error (RMSE), bias (the mean difference between point estimates and the estimand) and empirical standard error (standard deviation of point estimates).

Performance of 95% HDCIs or confidence intervals were summarised using coverage, the percentage of occasions that the intervals contained the estimand (true reliability value). A well-calibrated 95% HDCI should contain the true population parameter in 95% of the simulations (Rubin, 1984). We also report the mean HDCI length in the Supplement for each simulation condition.

Analysis

Simulation and analysis code was written in R and Stan. All models were fitted using the Bayesian probabilistic programming language Stan (Stan Development Team, 2024). To calculate RMU, we used the procedure outlined above, point estimates for RMU were computed using posterior means. All RMU uncertainty intervals were calculated using the highest density continuous interval, using the hdci function from the ggdist R package (Kay, 2024).

Because each pair of datasets was generated from the same simulated subjects, estimates from the two fits are not independent, so standard errors for all performance measures were calculated using cluster-robust (CR2) variance estimates clustered on simulation replicate (Pustejovsky et al., 2025).

Simulations were run using high performance computing clusters (King's College London, 2022). The number of simulations in each study varies due to computation time and available resources and is described in the respective study sections below and supplementary tables.

Across all three studies, Bayesian models were fitted using Stan's No-U-Turn sampler. All models were fitted using cmd-stanR (CmdStan v2.39.0; Gabry et al., 2023), either directly using Stan code, or using the brms R package (Bürkner, 2017). Each simulation used two chains with 1,000 warm-up iterations and 1,000 post-warm-up iterations per chain. The target average acceptance probability was set to .95, except in the smallest sample size condition of Study 3 (60 subjects) and throughout Study 1, where it was increased to .98.

We report the percentage of models with potential model fitting issues in each study using two diagnostics. We report the percentage of simulations that had at least one divergent transition or an E-BFMI (energy Bayesian fraction of missing information) less than .20 (default threshold used by rstan; Guo et al., 2025). Divergent transitions can occur when there are areas of high curvature in the posterior distribution, which can lead to inaccurate sampling (Betancourt, 2018). Low E-BFMI similarly indicates potential issues in posterior sampling (Betancourt, 2018).

Simulation Study 1: Linear Factor Models

In Study 1, we developed a Bayesian continuous item response theory model to estimate RMU, and then compared its performance to existing reliability estimators developed for the linear factor model (coefficient alpha and coefficient H). We limited our focus to unidimensional models.

The linear factor model is widely used to model responses to questionnaires or tasks with a fixed set of items. Suppose N subjects complete an extraversion questionnaire with P items. Let 𝑦 𝑖𝑗 indicate a response from subject i on item j. The factor model assumes each response (𝑦 𝑖𝑗 ) is generated by a weighted combination of subject i's latent variable score 𝜃 𝑖 plus measurement error (𝜀 𝑖𝑗 ). The item loading (𝜆 𝑗 ) controls the influence of the latent factor on the observed measurement. An example unidimensional factor model, presented without item intercepts, is shown below:

Some model parameters need to be constrained for model identification (Bollen, 1989). The model can be constrained by assuming the residual terms (𝜀 𝑖𝑗 ) are uncorrelated, and that the latent factor and observed score variances are equal to one. These constraints also "standardise" the factor loadings. The squared standardised factor loading (𝜆 2 𝑗 ) indicates the reliability of item j, and the residual variance on item j (𝜎 2 𝜀 𝑗 ) is 1 -𝜆 2 𝑗 (Revelle & Condon, 2018). A weighted sum score of the items can be used to estimate each subject's latent score and its reliability can be calculated using the methods outlined below.

The linear factor model is usually estimated using factor analysis or structural equation modelling techniques that utilise the means and covariances of the items (Bollen, 1989; Mehta & Neale, 2005). Traditional factor scoring first estimates factor loadings, then uses subject responses on each item to calculate factor scores (Bartholomew et al., 2009; Estabrook & Neale, 2013). In contrast, item response theory models participants' responses to each item and estimates latent parameters for each individual. RMU can be estimated from the posterior distribution of each participant's latent variable directly from the item response theory model.

In this study, we compare RMU to two existing reliability measures designed for the linear factor model.

Coefficient H

To estimate subjects' latent variable scores in a factor model, one can use a weighted sum of items where weights are proportional to factor loadings. This approach maximises the correlation between estimated and true latent scores (Bartholomew et al., 2009; Hancock & Mueller, 2001; McNeish, 2018). The maximal weights for each item can be computed from the standardised factor loadings (𝑤 𝑗 = 𝜆 𝑗 1-𝜆 2 𝑗 ). The reliability of the optimally weighted items can be found using coefficient H (McNeish, 2018):

If one is interested in the reliability of an equally weighted sum score of the items, when the standardised loadings vary, Omega should be used instead (McNeish, 2018). We used coefficient H because it represents the reliability of an optimal estimate of each subject's latent scores -and is more comparable to estimates generated from the Bayesian measurement model.

Coefficient alpha

Alpha is one of the most widely used methods of estimating reliability (Cronbach & Shavelson, 2004), making it a natural benchmark for comparing the performance of RMU. It can be viewed as a special case of omega or coefficient H, as when the standardised factor loadings are identical (𝜆1 = 𝜆2 = … = 𝜆 P ), the item weights will also be identical. This condition is called tauequivalence. Therefore, the optimal linear combination of the items will be an equally weighted sum score. Alpha measures the reliability of the resulting sum score, and can be computed using the number of items (P), sum score variance (𝜎 2 𝑌 ) and the average covariance between items (𝜎; Green & Yang, 2009):

When the tau-equivalence assumption holds, population alpha and H are identical. Due to sampling variability when estimating factor loadings, coefficient alpha and H typically differ in finite samples. When the tau-equivalence assumption is not met, coefficient alpha is negatively biased (McNeish, 2018).

Estimand

Because our estimand is calculated using the Bayesian model, this might favour RMU over other estimators. As a sensitivity analysis, when comparing different estimators, we will additionally use maximal reliability as an estimand, calculated by applying coefficient H to the known simulation item loadings. Maximal reliability represents the reliability of an optimally weighted sum of the items (i.e., weighted by the known loadings). Maximal reliability will generally be higher than the classical test theory estimand in smaller samples. This is because when factor loadings are estimated with error in finite samples, the resulting latent variable estimates are not necessarily optimal (Aguirre-Urreta et al., 2019).

Methods

Data generation

We specified 7 factor loading conditions with varying number of items and loadings (see Figure 2 for factor loading values). For each factor loading condition, and at each of three simulation sample sizes (50, 250 and 1,000), we ran 6,058 simulations. Let 𝑦 𝑖𝑗 indicate a response from subject i on item j. Let 𝜆 𝑗 refer to the standardised item loading for item j. Data was generated as follows:

Simulated data was centred and scaled prior to analysis.

Analysis

Coefficient alpha and its confidence intervals were calculated using the ci.reliability function from MBESS R package (Kelley, 2025). Coefficient H was estimated using two methods. The first estimator (H FA) was calculated using minimum residual factor analysis loadings estimated using the psych R package (Revelle, 2015). Confidence intervals were calculated using a percentile bootstrap procedure with 1000 bootstrap resamples.

We chose this approach because in practice, coefficient H is typically estimated from exploratory or confirmatory factor models. On testing, the minimal residual approach was faster than maximum likelihood methods, which is important because across all simulations 127 million bootstrapped models were fitted. The second estimator (H IRT) used the factor loadings from the Bayesian item response theory model outlined below. H IRT was calculated using each posterior draw of the loadings, generating 2000 posterior draws for H, which were then summarised using a posterior mean and 95% HDCI. We added H IRT to the analyses to test whether differences in performance were driven by the method of estimating the loadings. Because coefficient H is usually computed from exploratory or confirmatory factor models, H FA -not H IRT -reflects how H is typically applied in the literature.

We adapted an item response theory model for continuous responses to estimate RMU (Mellenbergh, 2016), which is outlined below. We specified hierarchical priors on the loading parameters, which greatly reduced the number of model-fitting issues, such as divergences and low E-BFMI warnings, compared to a flat prior specification.

Let 𝑦 𝑖𝑗 indicate a response from subject i on item j. Let 𝜆 𝑗 refer to the factor loading for item j. Model likelihoods and priors are as follows:

The model assumes our observed scores have a normal distribution with a mean of 𝜆 𝑗 𝜃 𝑖 , and SD of 𝜎 𝑗.

Results

Note.

The grey violin plots show the distribution of RMU reliability estimates. Red crosses indicate the mean RMU reliability estimate, and red circles indicate the target estimand computed from test-retest simulations. The headers on each subplot indicate the standardised factor loadings used in the simulations.

We analysed 127,218 simulated datasets across 21 conditions, with 7 sets of item loadings and three simulation sample sizes.

Figure 2 displays the distribution of RMU point estimates across all simulations and key performance measures. A red circle shows the target estimand for each condition. A dashed horizontal line indicates maximal reliability. Full results are also provided in Supplement Table 1. Sampler diagnostics indicated that model fitting issues were relatively rare (see Supplement Table 1).

When compared to the primary (test-retest) estimand, overall bias for RMU was low (Bias = .007) and accuracy was good (RMSE = .082), and coverage of the 95% HDCIs were close to nominal levels (Coverage = 93.8%; see Table 1 for confidence intervals). As shown in Figure 2, performance varied across the simulation conditions. In some conditions coverage was low even at larger sample sizes, particularly where the item loadings varied. This may be because the hierarchical priors for the loadings pool higher and lower estimates towards the group mean.

Estimates were slightly positively biased when the standardised item loadings were all zero (top left panel of Figure 2). Bias was .111 at the smallest sample size (nobs = 50) and decreased to .023 (nobs = 1,000). Because the posterior mean of RMU is effectively bounded below by zero (see Theoretical Properties of RMU), some positive bias is inevitable when the estimand is zero. The primary estimand (simulated test-retest reliability) was similar to or lower than maximal reliability, depending on the simulation condition. The gap was larger when the population item loadings varied and at smaller simulation sample sizes, where there is increased uncertainty in the factor loadings.

Comparison to coefficient alpha and H

We compared RMU to three alternative reliability estimators: alpha, factor analysis coefficient H (H FA), and item response theory coefficient H (H IRT). The distribution of sample estimates is provided in Figure 3, and overall performance measures are provided in Table 1. Performance metrics in each simulation condition can be found in Supplementary Table 1.

Performance statistics for each estimator are shown in Table 1. On most performance metrics, RMU and item response theory H estimated from the same Bayesian models performed similarly. As expected, given the lack of tau-equivalence in our simulations, alpha generally performed poorly compared to RMU. Figure 3 demonstrates that alpha generally underestimated maximal reliability when the population item loadings varied. However, as expected, alpha performed well when the population item loadings were equivalent across items (i.e., tauequivalent).

Factor analysis coefficient H performed poorly overall, with high error and substantial bias with respect to both the primary and secondary estimands (see Table 1). Even alpha performed much better than factor coefficient H. Figure 3 shows that factor analysis H performed poorly across most conditions. When all the loadings were zero (and our reliability estimand was zero) and when simulating a sample size of 50, the smallest factor analysis coefficient H we obtained was .269. One issue with factor analysis H was Heywood cases, where one standardised item loading was equal to 1 leading to reliability estimates of 1 (occurring in 4.7% of fits). However, removing Heywood cases has minimal impact on overall accuracy or bias (see https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/2_study1_heywood_removed.html), and Figure 3 shows that estimates are generally imprecise. In simulation conditions with stronger factor loadings and larger sample sizes (nobs = 1000) all four methods yielded similar results (see Figure 3).

Interim discussion

RMU calculated from a Bayesian continuous item response theory model yielded good reliability estimates and was more accurate than two alternative methods (alpha and factor analysis coefficient H). RMU 95% HDCIs contained the true reliability estimate approximately 95% of the time (i.e., exhibited nominal coverage). RMU performed better not only with the primary estimand (which is estimated from the Bayesian model fits) but also with the secondary maximal reliability estimand, which is not estimated from the Bayesian models (note that both estimands converge at larger sample sizes). Coefficient H simply defines how factor loadings can be combined to estimate reliability. How those factors are estimated impacts performance. Coefficient H estimated from minimal residual factor analysis performed poorly, whereas H estimated from the Bayesian item response theory model performed similarly to RMU. Thus, while RMU is not necessarily a better estimator than IRT coefficient H, RMU can be applied much more broadly, using the same procedure for models where no equivalent of coefficient H exists. Coefficient alpha is known to be biased when the factor loadings vary (McNeish, 2018), however despite this, it was significantly more accurate than factor analysis coefficient H. While some have advocated for more complex linear factor reliability estimators (e.g., coefficient H, Omega) over alpha, these alternatives may be more susceptible to overfitting and bias at small sample sizes (Aguirre-Urreta et al., 2019; Cho, 2021 Cho, , 2022;; Edwards et al., 2021). Researchers may prefer a conservative, low-variance estimator, even if it slightly underestimates reliability, over one that is asymptotically unbiased but imprecise in small samples. Aguirre-Urreta et al. (2019) showed that when unbiased estimates of the factor loadings are used, estimation error in these statistics will lead to bias in H. Their simulation results also found that H was positively biased at small sample sizes. One possible explanation why item response theory coefficient H performed better is that we specified hierarchical priors which regularise loadings towards the group mean, inducing some bias but reducing overfitting. Because coefficient H is typically estimated from exploratory or confirmatory factor analysis models (Cho, 2022; Revelle, 2015), the performance results from item response theory H do not reflect how H is typically used in research.

As expected, we found that simulated test-retest reliability from the Bayesian models increased slightly at larger sample sizes, converging to maximal reliability. At larger sample sizes, the factor loadings will be estimated with more precision, increasing reliability. This highlights the role of sample size in determining not only the accuracy of reliability estimates but also magnitude, particularly in more complex modelling scenarios.

Simulation Study 2: Signal Detection Theory Model

Signal detection theory is a framework for modelling human decision-making (Kellen et al., 2021; Macmillan & Creelman, 2005). Signal detection theory can be used to understand how features of stimuli influence subjects' classification decisions and model individual differences in subjects' ability to discriminate between stimuli.

In signal detection theory, the "correct" response varies depending on the trial condition. In a two-alternative forced choice signal detection theory experiment, subjects are presented with two kinds of stimuli (A or B), and can either respond A or B. In condition A, subjects should respond A; in condition B, subjects should respond B.

Consider the following memory recognition experiment, illustrated in Table 2. Participants are shown a set of images and then tested with a new set of images, including a mix of previously seen and new, unseen stimuli. In the testing phase, each trial has four possible outcomes: participants may correctly recognise a previously seen image ("hit"), they may fail to recognise a previously seen image ("miss"), they may also falsely recognise an unseen image ("false alarm"), or they may correctly identify the unseen image as unseen ("correct rejection"). A problem with simple metrics such as the hit rate (percentage of A responses in condition A) is that participants A more appropriate metric would also account for the false alarm rate on the task. Researchers are often interested in measuring how well participants shift their response according to the stimuli presented, known as sensitivity or d'. Sensitivity (d') can be computed using the probit-transformed (Φ -1 (𝑥)) Hit Rate (percentage of hits in the seen condition) and False Alarm Rate (percentage of false alarms in the unseen condition), see equation 9 below. Hit or False alarm rates of exactly 0 or 1 lead to infinite values, so these can be adjusted by assuming each participant had at least one hit, miss, false alarm and correct rejection.

One can also model response bias (κ) towards A or B responses. For a two-alternative forced choice signal detection theory task, sensitivity (d') and bias (κ) can be modelled using a multilevel probit binomial regression model (Rouder et al., 2007; Vuorre, 2017), as outlined in Analysis below. The random slope for condition measures how well participants shift their response according to the condition, and the random intercept captures any consistent response biases towards A or B.

In this study, we focused on estimating the reliability of the sensitivity parameter d', although RMU can also be applied to the bias parameter κ. We focused on sensitivity as it assesses overall accuracy on the task, and thus individual differences in sensitivity are more commonly of interest in applied research. We compared the performance of RMU to split-half reliability.

Methods

The target estimand for reliability was calculated using the same simulated test-retest procedure outlined in General Meth ods.

Data Generation

We used a factorial simulation design. Across all simulations, the population mean sensitivity and bias values were fixed at 𝜇 𝑑 ′ = .5 and 𝜇 𝜅 = 0, respectively. Between-person bias SD was fixed at 𝜎 𝜅 = .2. Trials were evenly split between conditions A and B. We varied the simulation sample sizes (nobs = 50, 250, 1000), number of trials (Ntrials = 20, 40, 80) and between-subject variance in sensitivity (𝜎 𝑑 ′ = 0, 𝜎 𝑑 ′ = .2, or 𝜎 𝑑 ′ = .40). When 𝜎 𝑑 ′ = 0, there are no individual differences in the true sensitivity values, and the population reliability for sensitivity is zero. As we ran a fully factorial design, there were 27 possible combinations of the above parameters, and each simulation was repeated 11,468 times in each condition.

Analysis

To calculate split-half reliability, we randomly divided each subject's responses into two split half datasets, computed sensitivity for each subject in each half dataset (using equation 9), and then computed alpha on each split-half dataset using the same approach as Study 1 (Novick & Lewis, 1967; Pronk et al., 2022; Revelle & Condon, 2018). Computing sensitivity directly from the probit-transformed hit and false alarm rates yields very similar results to the Bayesian approach (see https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/tutorial_calculating_rmu_gonogo.html#appendix-a-bayesian-vs-simple-d-estimates comparing results from both approaches). Like Study 1, we computed maximum likelihood confidence intervals using the MBESS R package to compute alpha on split-half estimates (Kelley, 2025). Alpha or H cannot be directly applied to each subject's responses because sensitivity is not computed using a sum score. Note that alpha-corrected split-half reliability slightly differs from Spearman-Brown corrected reliability which uses standardised alpha (Cortina, 1993).

We used a Bayesian random intercept and slope probit binomial regression model, fitted using the brms R package (Bürkner, 2017).

Let 𝑛 𝑗𝑖 indicate the number of trials from subject i in condition j. Let 𝑦 𝑖1 and 𝑦 𝑖2 indicate the number of false alarms and hits for subject i. Condition was contrast-coded so that, for condition B trials condition 𝑖,𝑗=2 = -1 2 , and for condition A trials condition 𝑖,𝑗=1 = 1 2 . Model likelihoods and priors are as follows:

For the above model, the bias parameter is equal to the negative random intercept (𝜅 𝑖 = -(𝛽 0 + 𝛽 1𝑖 )) and the sensitivity parameter is equal to the random slope (𝑑 ′ 𝑖 = 𝛽 cond + 𝛽 2𝑖 ). We used weakly informative priors, including an LKJ Distribution prior (η = 1) for the correlation between random effects (Lewandowski et al., 2009).

Results

Note.

The grey violin plots show the distribution of RMU reliability estimates. Red crosses indicate the mean RMU reliability estimate, and red circles indicate the target estimand computed from testretest simulations. We ran 309,636 simulations across 27 conditions varying the number of trials and variation in population sensitivity. Detailed results in each condition are presented in Figure 4 and Supplement Table 2.

Overall performance of RMU was good, with low bias (.017, 95% CI [.017, .018]) and close to nominal coverage (96.4%, 95% CI [96.4%, 96.5%]). Model-fitting issues were uncommon, with few divergent transitions (occurring in only 0.6% of simulations) and no cases of low E-BFMI.

As with Study 1, when population variance in sensitivity was zero (and thus population reliability is also zero), RMU sample estimates were slightly positively biased, and coverage was slightly above nominal levels. In some conditions (e.g., 80 trials, Sensitivity SD = .20), RMU was slightly negatively biased at small sample sizes (nobs = 50), with bias decreasing at larger sample sizes.

Comparison to split-half reliability

Figure 5 gives an overview of the relative accuracy and precision of RMU and split-half reliability in each condition (see Supplement Table 2 for more detail). Overall, RMU was more accurate (RMSE = .084) than split-half (RMSE = .158), with a relative RMSE of 88.1%. The relative RMSE indicates the relative difference in error between split-half and RMU estimators (.158 = .084 + 88.1% × .084; Morris et al., 2019). Similarly, RMU was more precise (EmpSe = .211) than split-half (EmpSe = .274), with a relative precision of 29.9%. The difference between RMU and split-half in accuracy was more notable in conditions with fewer trials, smaller simulation sample sizes and lower population variability in sensitivity. At a sample size of 1000, the differences in accuracy between RMU and splithalf were moderate (all relative RMSE < 49%). Figure 5 also highlights that split-half reliability yielded estimates of less than zero in some conditions, unlike RMU. This may explain why split-half reliability is less susceptible to positive bias when the population reliability is zero: split-half estimates are distributed roughly symmetrically around zero, whereas RMU estimates are effectively bounded below by it.

Coverage was good for both RMU (Coverage = 96.4%, 95% CI [96.4%, 96.5%]) and split-half reliability (Coverage = 94.2%, 95% CI [94.1%, 94.2%]). The average confidence interval/HDCI length was larger for RMU (HDCI Length = .414) compared to split-half (CI length = .323), though this is because the latter truncates the lower bound at zero. In conditions with very low reliability (particularly when Sensitivity SD was 0), RMU exhibited over-coverage and had longer interval lengths than split-half (see Supplementary Table 2 for details). Note. The left, red half of each violin plot indicates the distribution of RMU estimates, and the right, blue half indicates the distribution of split-half estimates. Densities are normalized to the same width. The relative standard error (RMSE or EmpSE) indicates the percentage increase in the standard error of splithalf estimates relative to RMU. A 20% relative standard error indicates that the standard error of split-half is 20% greater than the RMU standard error (𝑆𝐸 split-half = 𝑆𝐸 RMU + 20% • 𝑆𝐸 RMU ).

Interim Discussion

For estimating reliability of the sensitivity parameter in signal detection theory models, we found that RMU performed well on most performance measures, including bias, accuracy and coverage. On most performance measures, RMU was superior to split-half reliability, particularly at smaller sample sizes and number of trials.

The reduced accuracy of split-half reliability might partly be attributable to the additional Monte Carlo error introduced by the random allocation of trials to each split-half. Considering all possible split halves may help to reduce this variability and improve the precision of the reliability estimates. Indeed, under certain conditions, coefficient alpha is equivalent to the average split-half reliability over all possible splits (Lord & Novick, 1968, p. 93). An alternative approach to split-half estimation involves bootstrap resampling each participant's trial data to generate pseudo-test-retest observations (Pronk et al., 2022; Williams & Kaufmann, 2012). Future research could compare the performance of RMU to these more sophisticated resampling approaches.

Again, it is worth emphasising that the primary benefit of RMU over split-half reliability, in our view, is not just about accuracy, but that it can be flexibly applied across a wide range of models. RMU can be extended to more complex signal detection theory models; for example, one could include additional covariates to control for extraneous factors such as time of day or control for changes in sensitivity over the testing session. Implementing resampling methods such as split-half or bootstrapping is more challenging with these more complex models.

Simulation Study 3: Reinforcement Learning Model

In the behavioural and neurosciences, reinforcement learning models are used to understand the effects of rewards on trialand-error learning and its neural mechanisms (Ludvig et al., 2011). Individual differences in reinforcement learning model parameters have been related to several psychological traits, such as internalising (V. M. Brown et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2024) and ADHD (Ziegler et al., 2016) symptomatology.

Despite the widespread use of reinforcement learning models, there is a lack of established methods for assessing reliability. Reliability measures derived from the linear factor model (e.g., alpha, omega, H) cannot be applied to trial-level reinforcement learning data. Moreover, applying split-half or other resampling techniques is challenging because learning from the previous trials influences performance in subsequent trials. Split-half reliability assessments are possible if there are differentiated blocks of data with different stimuli to learn (e.g., Cheng et al., 2024). Consequently, researchers have primarily relied on test-retest assessments to evaluate the reliability of these models (Mkrtchian et al., 2023; Schaaf et al., 2023; Vrizzi et al., 2023). However, because reliability estimates are not portable across different populations and experimental tasks, it is essential for researchers employing these computational methods in individual differences research to have access to methods for calculating reliability in one's own study, even if retest data has not been collected.

In Study 3, we evaluated the performance of RMU in the context of a reinforcement learning model applied to a two-armed bandit task. The two-armed bandit task mimics a gambler playing at two slot machines with the same reward and cost of playing, but each machine has a different reward probability. Here, one arm has a reward probability of around 75%, and the other has a reward probability of around 25%. Because participants do not know the true reward probabilities, they must explore each arm to learn which machine has the higher payout probability.

We employed a Rescorla-Wagner reinforcement learning model with two subject parameters: learning rate and decision noise. We focused on estimating the reliability of the learning rate parameter. We chose a simple reinforcement learning model to reduce compute time. However, RMU could also be applied to more advanced models that account for additional behavioural features observed in the task (e.g., Palminteri & Lebreton, 2021).

Methods

Data Generation

We used a factorial simulation design varying the simulation sample size (60, 120, 240), number of trials (Ntrials = 90, 180, 320) and learning rate standard deviation (0, .070, .138) across conditions. The maximum simulation sample size was limited to 240 to reduce computation time. Across all conditions, arms had fixed reward probabilities (25% or 75%) and rewards (2point reward or -1-point penalty).

To match the analysis model, learning rates and inverse decision noise values for each subject were generated by drawing from a normal distribution and then applying the inverse probit function. Across all simulation conditions, the population mean learning rate was fixed at .2. The population mean of the inverse decision noise parameter was fixed at .75 with a standard deviation of .058 on the latent scale; after the probit transformation, this parameter is constrained to the range 0 to 5. Study 3 included fewer simulations due to the substantially longer computation time required for each model. The number of simulations varied from 2,218 to 6,430 depending on the condition (see Supplementary Table 3).

Analysis

Stan code for the reinforcement learning model was adapted from the hBayesDM R package (Ahn et al., 2017), and models were fitted using cmdstanr (Gabry et al., 2023).

Let choice 𝑖𝑗 represent the selected arm (1 or 2) by subject i on trial j. Subject-level learning rate (𝛼 𝑖 ) and inverse decision noise (𝜏 𝑖 ; also known as inverse temperature) parameters were modelled using latent normal distributions. The probit link function was used to constrain the learning rate between 0 and 1, and the inverse decision noise (𝜏 𝑖 ) parameter between 0 and 5. 𝑄 𝑖𝑗 = {𝑞 1𝑖𝑗 , 𝑞 2𝑖𝑗 } represents reward expectations for arms 1 and 2, for subject i on trial j, and is updated during each trial. Model likelihoods and priors are as follows: choice 𝑖𝑗 ∼ Categorical (softmax (𝜏 𝑖 𝑄 𝑖𝑗 )), choice 𝑖𝑗 ∈ {1, 2} 𝛼 𝑖 = 𝜙(𝛼 * 𝑖 ), where0 ≤ 𝛼 𝑖 ≤ 1 𝜏 𝑖 = 5𝜙(𝜏 * 𝑖 ), where0 ≤ 𝜏 𝑖 ≤ 5 𝛼 * 𝑖 ∼ Normal (𝜇 * 𝛼 , 𝜎 * 𝛼 ) 𝜏 * 𝑖 ∼ Normal (𝜇 * 𝜏 , 𝜎 * 𝜏 ) (11) Hyperpriors: 𝜇 * 𝛼 , 𝜇 * 𝜏 ∼ Normal (0, 1) 𝜎 * 𝛼 , 𝜎 * 𝜏 ∼ Normal (0, 0.2) (12) Updating of reward expectations (𝑄 𝑖𝑗 ) and prediction error (𝛿 𝑖𝑗 ) on each trial: 𝑄 𝑖𝑗 = {0, 0}, for 𝑗 = 1 𝛿 𝑖𝑗 [choice 𝑖𝑗 ] = reward 𝑖𝑗 -𝑄 𝑖𝑗 [choice 𝑖𝑗 ], for 𝑗 > 1 𝑄 𝑖,𝑗+1 [choice 𝑖𝑗 ] = 𝑄 𝑖𝑗 [choice 𝑗𝑖 ] + 𝛼 𝑖 × 𝛿 𝑖𝑗 [choice 𝑖𝑗 ], for 𝑗 > 1 (13) choice 𝑖𝑗 is modelled using a log-odds scaled categorical distribution.

The probability of a participant selecting the 1 st or 2 nd arm is calculated by multiplying the participant's inverse decision noise parameter (𝜏 𝑖 ) by the reward expectation vector (𝑄 𝑖𝑗 ), which is then transformed by the softmax function.

When inverse decision noise decreases, subjects are more likely to choose each arm randomly (50%/50%). When inverse decision noise increases, subjects are more likely to select the arm with the higher reward expectation.

The key feature of the reinforcement learning model is how subjects' reward expectations for each arm (𝑄 𝑖𝑗 ) are updated on each trial. On the first trial, reward expectations are initialised at 0 (𝑄 𝑖1 = {0, 0}). Once a subject has selected an arm and an outcome is observed, the model calculates the prediction error (𝛿 𝑖𝑗 ), the difference between the selected arm's reward/ punishment value and the expected reward for the chosen arm (𝛿 𝑖𝑗 [choice 𝑖𝑗 ] = reward 𝑖𝑗 -𝑄 𝑖𝑗 [choice 𝑖𝑗 ]). The arm's expected reward on the following trial is then updated by multiplying the subject-specific learning rate by the prediction error (𝑄 𝑖,𝑗+1 [choice 𝑖𝑗 ] = 𝑄 𝑖𝑗 [choice 𝑖𝑗 ] + 𝛼 𝑖 × 𝛿 𝑖𝑗 [choice 𝑖𝑗 ]).

As outlined above, we used the default priors from the hBayesDM R package for the standard deviation and mean of the population learning rate and decision noise parameters.

Results

Note.

The grey violin plots show the distribution of RMU reliability estimates. Red crosses indicate the mean RMU reliability estimate, and red circles indicate the target estimand computed from test-retest simulations.

We ran 119,722 simulations across 27 different conditions with varying trial numbers and population learning rate variabilities. RMU performance in each condition is described in Figure 6, and detailed results with Monte Carlo confidence intervals are provided in Supplement Table 3. Issues with divergent transitions or low E-BFMI were rare, affecting only 43 fits.

Overall, RMU performed well, with small average bias (-.023, 95% CI [-.024, -.023]), good accuracy (RMSE = .085, 95% CI [ .084, .086]), and slightly conservative coverage (96.4%, 95% CI [96.3%, 96.5%]). Bias was larger in individual conditions (up to -.106), as described below.

Performance varied slightly across conditions. As with the previous studies, when the estimand was zero, RMU was slightly positively biased and HDCIs exhibited over-coverage. This is unlikely to be of practical concern because the magni-tude of bias was small and the distribution of point estimates was narrowly clustered near zero. Furthermore, when the estimand was zero, HDCIs nearly always included zero (coverage ≥ .993).

When the estimand was greater than zero, Figure 6 shows that RMU was slightly negatively biased, though bias diminished as the number of trials or simulation sample size increased. At simulation sample sizes of 60, 120, and 240, the average 95% HDCI lengths were .445, .313 and .223, respectively.

Interim Discussion

In Study 3, we evaluated the performance of RMU applied to a two-armed bandit task analysed using a Rescorla-Wagner reinforcement learning model. We assessed the performance of RMU to estimate the reliability of individual differences in learning rates. Overall, RMU yielded generally accurate point estimates and well-calibrated HDCIs. In some conditions, at smaller simulation sample sizes, RMU estimates were slightly conservative (lower than the estimand), with this bias reducing in larger sample sizes.

The extensive time required to fit each model prevented us from testing performance with larger sample sizes. At large sample sizes, faster methods for approximating the posterior distribution such as automatic variational inference may be required, which may impact the performance of RMU. Even at a sample size of 60, the average 95% HDCI was relatively wide (.445). This suggests that reliability estimates may be too uncertain to be informative at much smaller sample sizes, which are common in computational research. This highlights the importance of reporting uncertainty alongside point estimates.

General Discussion

Reliability is a fundamental property of psychological measurement, yet methods for evaluating it have not kept pace with the increasing popularity of more complex models of behaviour. Existing techniques, such as coefficient alpha and H, are limited to estimating the reliability of (weighted) sum scores of a fixed set of items and assume a linear factor model generates the item responses. In this paper, we introduced a novel method for estimating reliability that can be widely applied across Bayesian measurement models, called relative measurement uncertainty (RMU). RMU involves randomly selecting samples from subjects' posterior and calculating the correlation between pairs of draws. Although RMU shares similarities with the empirical reliability method (Du Toit, 2003), our method also yields a full posterior distribution for reliability estimates -crucial for communicating uncertainty in small studies. Simulation results suggest that RMU yields generally accurate and well-calibrated reliability estimates and uncertainty intervals across linear factor, signal detection theory and reinforcement learning models. In the accompanying https://github.com/giac01/8_bayes_reliability we provide code and tutorials illustrating how to apply RMU to several different generative models.

RMU generally matched or outperformed existing methods, including alpha, H, and split-half reliability, in terms of accuracy and coverage. Alpha performed comparably to RMU except in simulation conditions with varying item loadings, which violates its tau-equivalence assumption (McNeish, 2018). This highlights that RMU's advantage is that it is not limited to a specific measurement model and can be flexibly adapted. In the Applied Examples section, we illustrate how RMU can be applied to data with varying numbers of measurements per subject and measurement censoring. Consistent with previous research (Aguirre-Urreta et al., 2019; Cho, 2021; Edwards et al., 2021), in Study 1, we found that coefficient H estimated using minimum residual factor analysis was highly inaccurate, with both high bias and variance. However, coefficient H performed as well as RMU when the loadings are estimated from a Bayesian item response theory model with regularised loadings. It is worth noting again that, unlike RMU, coefficient H can only be applied to linear factor models.

In Study 2, we found that RMU yielded more accurate reliability estimates than split-half reliability for the sensitivity signal detection theory parameter, particularly at small sample sizes. In the Applied Examples section we also compared RMU and split-half estimates of reliability with data from a fluctuating bandit task, which yielded slightly different results. One limitation of split-half methods is that deciding how to split or resample the trial-level data can substantially impact the analysis (Pronk et al., 2022). This can limit where split-half and other resampling methods can be used. In the case of large Bayesian models, refitting the data additional times on splithalf or bootstrap resampled datasets may be computationally demanding.

Two systematic patterns emerged across all three simulation studies and warrant comment. First, when population reliability was zero, RMU point estimates were slightly positively biased and HDCIs over-covered. This follows from the theoretical properties of RMU: because the point estimates are effectively bounded below by zero, sampling variability will push estimates upwards when the true reliability is zero. However, in these conditions the HDCIs often included zero, and the distribution of point estimates was narrowly clustered near zero. We therefore recommend that researchers should routinely report uncertainty intervals or plot the full posterior alongside the RMU point estimate. Split-half estimates, which can take negative values and are distributed roughly symmetrically around zero, did not show this bias, though at the cost of higher variance.

Limitations

While our results are promising, we have not tested RMU under an exhaustive range of conditions, and more research is needed to understand potential limitations. One obvious limitation is the slightly greater computational demands compared to (overly) simplistic measures -but these are rarely prohibitively burdensome even for laptop based computing. Future work could also explore the relative strengths and weaknesses of RMU compared to other alternative methods beyond split-half reliability, such as bootstrap resampling (Pronk et al., 2022). Future research could also more extensively compare estimates derived from different methods, including RMU, to test-retest reliability estimates using real data.

Model-based reliability estimates like RMU should be cautiously interpreted as they depend on a well-specified generative model of the responses. This is a fundamental consideration for most existing model-based reliability estimators. For example, coefficient alpha assumes each item has the same factor loading, which is often violated in practice (Graham, 2006; McNeish, 2018). Researchers should carefully consider whether the models employed are appropriate for their specific data and research questions.

Conclusion

In this paper, we developed and evaluated a novel Bayesian method for reliability estimation that is particularly wellsuited for complex behavioural assessments. While our results demonstrate that this approach can outperform several traditional reliability metrics in terms of accuracy, its most significant contribution is its versatility. This flexibility enables researchers to report reliability and its uncertainty across a substantially broader range of experimental paradigms and computational models than was previously feasible.

Theoretical Properties of RMU This section analytically derives two properties of RMU, both in the limiting case of an infinite number of subjects. First, we show that the RMU point estimate equals empirical reliability when both are computed from the same posterior distributions. As a corollary of the first result, the RMU point estimate cannot be negative in this limit. Second, for a simple multilevel model with known parameters and a closed-form posterior distribution, we show that RMU equals the classical test theory reliability of the mean score.

RMU and Empirical reliability Framework and notation

Let N denote the number of subjects. Measurement data is collected from each subject and Bayesian modelling is used to quantify uncertainty in each subject's true value on a latent variable (𝜃) for which we aim to estimate reliability. Let 𝑝 𝑖 (𝜃), 𝐸[𝜃 | 𝐼 = 𝑖] and Var [𝜃 | 𝐼 = 𝑖] denote the latent variable marginal posterior distribution, posterior mean and posterior variance for subject i. Let θ denote the length N vector of posterior means for each subject in the sample ( θ = θ1 , θ2 , …, θN ) and let 𝜎 2 θ denote the variance of posterior means. Let V represent the average within-subject posterior variance across all subjects (

Let 𝜽 * 𝐣 denote a length N vector containing one posterior draw for each subject, 𝜽 * 𝐣 = 𝜃 * 𝑗1 , 𝜃 * 𝑗2 , …, 𝜃 * 𝑗N . We assume that, for each subject i, the draws 𝜃 * 𝑗𝑖 and 𝜃 * 𝑘𝑖 (𝑗 ≠ 𝑘) are independent and identically distributed according to that subject's marginal posterior, 𝜃 * 𝑗𝑖 ∼ iid 𝑝 𝑖 (𝜃). In practice, each vector 𝜃 * 𝑗 is a single joint MCMC draw, so its elements share that iteration's draw of any population-level parameters and are not strictly independent across subjects. The results below depend only on each subject's marginal posterior, 𝑝 𝑖 (𝜃), and treat draws as independent across subjects. In typical hierarchical models this dependence diminishes as N increases, because the posterior of the population-level parameters concentrates, so it does not affect the limiting results. At finite N, it can produce small differences between the RMU point estimate and empirical reliability.

The RMU posterior draws (𝑟 1 , 𝑟 2 , …, 𝑟K 2 ) are computed from K 2 Pearson correlations between independent posterior draw vectors, 𝑟 𝑡 = cor (𝜃 * 𝑗 , 𝜃 * 𝑘 ). The RMU point estimate can be computed as the posterior mean, 𝑟 = 2K -1 ∑ K/2 𝑡=1 𝑟 𝑡 . We write 𝜌 for the corresponding population correlation, i.e., the correlation between 𝜃 * 𝑗𝑖 and 𝜃 * 𝑘𝑖 when i is selected at random. With finite N, each 𝑟 𝑡 is a noisy estimate of 𝜌. As N → ∞, every 𝑟 𝑡 converges to 𝜌, so the RMU posterior collapses onto ρ and the point estimate equals ρ.

Empirical reliability is the ratio of posterior mean variance divided by the sum of the posterior mean variance and average within-subject posterior variance:

In this section, we assume empirical reliability is computed using the same posterior distributions as RMU.

Theorem 1

For simplicity, we will consider the case where we have an infinite sample size (N = ∞). In this case, we can show that the pointestimate of RMU equals empirical reliability:

Proof of Theorem 1

To derive 𝜌 (Cor (𝜃 * 𝑗 , 𝜃 * 𝑘 )), we use the law of total covariance to find the covariance between 𝜃 * 𝑗 and 𝜃 * 𝑘 , and the law of total variance to find their variances. Here, expectations, variances and covariances are taken over a randomly selected subject i and the random draws. Because draws j and k are independent conditional on subject

The correlation of 𝜃 * 𝑗 and 𝜃 * 𝑘 is found by dividing their covariance (𝜎 2 θ ) by their variance (𝜎 2 θ + V ).

Equation 18 is identical to empirical reliability (Equation 14). Since every 𝑟 𝑡 converges to 𝜌 as N → ∞, the RMU point estimate converges to empirical reliability under the assumptions above.

Corollary

Since 𝜎 2 θ ≥ 0 and V ≥ 0, 𝜌 must also be non-negative. Therefore, the point-estimate for RMU is also non-negative in the limit. With finite N, individual 𝑟 𝑡 and hence the lower limit of the credible interval, may be negative.

RMU applied to a multilevel model Framework and Notation

We assume an infinite sample size of subjects (N = ∞), allowing us to disregard sampling error. In this example, each subject is measured T times, and we are interested in estimating reliability of subjects' mean scores. Let 𝑦 𝑖𝑚 indicate a single measurement m from subject i. Each measurement is distributed as:

Where 𝜃 𝑖 indicates the expected (or "true score") value for subject i, and we assume constant measurement variance across subjects (𝜎 2 𝜀 ). Assume the true scores are normally distributed across subjects with a known population mean (𝜇) and variance (𝜎 2 𝜃 ):

Let 𝐲 denote the vector of all subject's observed mean scores (𝐲 = 𝑦 1 , 𝑦 2 , …, 𝑦 N ; where 𝑦 𝑖 = T -1 ∑ T 𝑚=1 𝑦 𝑖𝑚 ). The reliability of the mean scores is well-known in classical test theory (CTT; Levy & Mislevy, 2016, p. 165; Lord & Novick, 1968, p. 111):

Measurements are modelled using a multilevel model with known 𝜎 2 𝜀 , 𝜎 2 𝜃 and 𝜇 model parameters values (Gelman et al., 2021, p. 116; Levy & Mislevy, 2016, p. 168), which has a closed form posterior distribution. The model likelihood for each subject's mean score (𝑦 𝑖 ) and prior for the true scores are outlined below.

The posterior distribution for each subject's true score (𝜃 𝑖 ) is normally distributed with mean θ𝑖 and variance 𝑉 (Gelman et al., 2021, p. 116; Levy & Mislevy, 2016, p. 168): θ𝑖 = 1 𝜎 2 𝜀 T 𝑦 𝑖 + 1 𝜎 2 𝜃 𝜇 1 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 1 𝜎 2 𝜃 (25) 𝑉 = 1 1 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 1 𝜎 2 𝜃 = 𝜎 2 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜀 T 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 (26) Let 𝜽 * 𝐣 denote a length N vector of random draws from each subject's posterior (𝜽 * 𝐣 = 𝜃 * 𝑗1 , 𝜃 * 𝑗2 , …, 𝜃 * 𝑗N ).

Because the sample is infinite, RMU can be calculated without error by randomly drawing two vectors of posterior draws and calculating the correlation between them, RMU = Cor (𝜽 * 𝐣 , 𝜽 * 𝐤 ). Theorem 2 The RMU point estimate derived from the above multilevel model is equivalent to classical test theory reliability: 𝑟 = 𝜌 = Cor (𝜽 * 𝐣 , 𝜽 * 𝐤 ) = 𝜎 2 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜃 + 𝜎 2 𝜀 T = CTT Reliability (𝐲) (27) Proof of Theorem 2 To derive Cor (𝜽 * 𝐣 , 𝜽 * 𝐤 ), we first need to find Var ( θ), Var (𝜽 * 𝐣 ) and Cov (𝜽 * 𝐣 , 𝜽 * 𝐤 ). The posterior mean variance is smaller than the true score variance: Var ( θ) = Var ( 1 𝜎 2 𝜀 T 𝐲 + 𝜇 𝜎 2 𝜃 1 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 1 𝜎 2 𝜃 ) = Var ( 1 𝜎 2 𝜀 T 1 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 1 𝜎 2 𝜃 𝐲 ) = ( 𝜎 2 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 ) 2 Var (𝐲) = ( 𝜎 2 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 ) 2 ( 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 ) = 𝜎 4 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 (28) A vector of posterior draws 𝜽 * 𝐣 can be decomposed as the sum of the posterior means ( θ) and an error vector (𝝂 𝐣 ), such that 𝝂 𝐣 = 𝜈 𝑗1 , 𝜈 𝑗2 , …, 𝜈 𝑗N ∼ iid Normal (0, 𝑉 ). The variance of posterior draws corresponds to the true score variance (𝜎 2 𝜃 ): Var (𝜽 * 𝐣 ) = Var ( θ + 𝝂 𝐣 ) = Var ( θ) + Var (𝝂 𝐣 ) = 𝜎 4 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 + 𝜎 2 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜀 T 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 = 𝜎 2 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 4 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 = 𝜎 2 𝜃 ( 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 ) 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 = 𝜎 2 𝜃 (29) Since different posterior draws {𝜽 * 𝐣 , 𝜽 * 𝐤 } have independent error vectors (𝝂 𝐣 ⊥𝝂 𝐤 ), their covariance equals the posterior mean variance: Cov (𝜽 * 𝐣 , 𝜽 * 𝐤 ) = Cov ( θ + 𝝂 𝐣 , θ + 𝝂 𝐤 ) = Var ( θ) (30)

Finally, we can show that the correlation between two independent sets of random draws from each subject's posterior {𝜽 * 𝐣 , 𝜽 * 𝐤 } corresponds to the reliability of the mean score:

Cor (𝜽 * 𝐣 , 𝜽 * 𝐤 ) = Cov (𝜽 * 𝐣 , 𝜽 * 𝐤 ) Var (𝜽 * 𝐣 ) = Var ( θ) Var (𝜽 * 𝐣 ) = 𝜎 4 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜀 T + 𝜎 2 𝜃 /𝜎 2 𝜃 = 𝜎 2 𝜃 𝜎 2 𝜃 + 𝜎 2 𝜀 T = CTT Reliability (𝐲) (31)

Note that each participant's posterior mean ( θ𝑖 ) is a weighted combination of their mean score (𝑦 𝑖 ) and the population mean (𝜇). The posterior means ( θ𝑖 ) are weighted closer to the population mean when 𝜎 2 𝜀 T increases or the true score variance (𝜎 2 𝜃 ) decreases. This shrinkage (or regularization) improves accuracy by reducing variance while introducing only minimal bias (McElreath, 2020). The use of regularised posterior means does not bias RMU reliability estimates in this example (c.f., A. Brown & Croudace, 2014, p. 314). Similarly, in classical test theory, Kelley's formula indicates that true scores are best estimated by adjusting observed scores toward the population mean proportionally to the reliability coefficient (Levy & Mislevy, 2016, p. 158). Code and online materials

All code and data (excluding simulation results) can be found in the following GitHub repository https://github.com/giac01/8_bayes_reliability. Direct links to web and pdf versions of each applied example are listed below. The GitHub repository has also been archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23338878). Simulation result files are archived on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/23340581).

• Direct link to download the GitHub repository: https://github.com/giac01/8_bayes_reliability/archive/refs/heads/main.zip • Example 1 (mean score): https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/tutorial_rmu_sum_score_reliability.html https://github.com/giac01/8_bayes_reliability/blob/main/tutorial_rmu_sum_score_reliability.pdf • Example 2 (multi-armed bandit): https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/tutorial_calculating_rmu_bandit.html https://github.com/giac01/8_bayes_reliability/blob/main/tutorial_calculating_rmu_bandit.pdf • Example 3 (Go/No-Go, not in main manuscript): https://www.bignardi.co.uk/8_bayes_reliability/tutorial_calculating_rmu_gonogo.html https://github.com/giac01/8_bayes_reliability/blob/main/tutorial_calculating_rmu_gonogo.pdf The reinforcement learning example (Example 2) uses the Fluctuating Bandit task data from Pike et al. (2026) (https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291726105340). The https://osf.io/kde4b/ and https://osf.io/p648q/ are openly available on the Open Science Framework (CC BY 4.0). The Go/No-Go example (Example 3), which is reported only in the online documentation and not in the main manuscript, uses data from Hedge, Powell and Sumner (2018; https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0935-1), available at https://osf.io/cwzds/.
